newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich backs move to put off tax cuts - Post.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich backs move to put off tax cuts - Post.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich endorsed the idea Monday of putting off a major tax cut to help achieve a balanced budget deal with President Clinton, the Washington Post reported Tuesday.

Gingrich, speaking to a group of reporters, called his switch on the Republicans' drive for a big tax cut a tactical retreat that would deprive liberals of their favourite objection in the balanced budget debate.
At the same time, the Georgia Republican said, it would leave the GOP free to rejoin the campaign for lower taxes later, according to the report.
"We don't want to get into a trap where every time we propose any kind of healthy change in the government, liberals have automatic screaming about tax cuts," the newspaper quoted Gingrich as saying.
"So let's take tax cuts away for a moment. Let's just talk about balancing the budget. Now what's the liberal excuse for not balancing the budget?"
Gingrich's switch on the tax cut puts him at odds with Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi and House and Senate Republican tax-writing leaders.
Lott Monday said, "It's not my intent to have a package that doesnt have some appropriate tax relief for working Americans."
White House Budget Director Franklin Raines said Sunday Clinton will stick by the budget he submitted to Congress last month, rejecting calls from Republicans to completely revamp it.
He said that the White House hopes that it can strike a budget deal with Congress by April, despite complaints from Republicans that Clinton's proposed plan does not balance the budget by 2002.

Senate Budget Committee chairman Pete Dominici, a New Mexico Republican, said that he would offer a Republican alternative budget if Clinton did not make deeper cuts in entitlement programmes such as Medicare to balance the budget.

Clinton sent Congress a $1.69 trillion budget proposal that cut $98.4 billion in taxes over five years, slashed $100 billion from Medicare health care for the elderly and reached a $17 billion surplus in 2002.

In the last Congress, budget negotiations fell apart and forced two government shutdowns that the public blamed on Republicans, but Republicans initially spoke of bipartisanship in crafting a budget this year.
But those public statements of goodwill have eroded recently, with each party taking shots at the other over lack of visible progress on the budget.
